hooks: A portmanteau of Mexico and California — its twin across the border, Calexico, is the same two words the other way round.
It has the largest Chinese-descended community in Mexico, brought in to dig irrigation canals from 1903.
Its Chinatown, La Chinesca, has tunnels and basements built to escape the 50 °C summer heat.
Probably from a Kumeyaay word, tiwan, "by the sea", rather than the folk story about a woman called Tía Juana.
Its border crossing is one of the busiest in the world, with tens of millions of crossings a year.
The Caesar salad was invented here in 1924 by an Italian restaurateur during Prohibition.
Spanish for "cove" or "inlet".
Its Valle de Guadalupe produces about 70% of Mexican wine.
La Bufadora nearby is a marine geyser that shoots seawater 30 m up through a sea cave.
Renamed in 1888 for Benito Juárez, who governed Mexico from here during the French occupation.
It faces El Paso across the Rio Grande, forming one of the largest binational conurbations in the world.
Its maquiladora assembly plants employ hundreds of thousands of people making goods for the American market.
Named in 1828 for José María González Hermosillo, an independence general.
One of the hottest cities in Mexico, regularly above 48 °C in summer.
Ford has built cars here since 1986, and the city is the capital of Sonora.
From Nahuatl mazatl, "deer", plus -tlan — "place of deer".
Its carnival is one of the largest in the world, behind Rio and New Orleans.
It has the longest seafront promenade in Mexico, about 21 km.
Probably Nahuatl or Tarahumara for "dry sandy place" or "between two waters"; the dog is named after the state, not the other way round.
The largest state in Mexico, bigger than the United Kingdom.
Copper Canyon in it is deeper and larger than the Grand Canyon, and the railway through it climbs 2,400 m with 86 tunnels.
"New Laredo" — founded in 1848 by residents of Laredo who chose to stay Mexican after the border moved.
They dug up their dead and brought them across the river with them.
It is the largest inland port in Latin America, handling much of the trade between Mexico and the United States.
Named for Álvaro Obregón, a general and president assassinated in 1928.
It is the centre of the Yaqui valley, where Norman Borlaug bred the wheat that started the Green Revolution.
That work fed perhaps a billion people and won him the Nobel Peace Prize.
Named for Reinosa in Spain, the birthplace of a colonial official.
It is a major crossing point and a centre of natural gas production.
Its maquiladoras make a large share of Mexico’s electronics exports.
Named for Mariano Matamoros, a priest and independence fighter executed in 1814.
The first battles of the Mexican-American War were fought just outside it in 1846.
It faces Brownsville, Texas, across the Rio Grande.
From a Cahita word for a land turtle, or for a flowering plant.
It is the Pacific terminus of the Copper Canyon railway, which climbs 2,400 m with 86 tunnels.
The town was founded around a sugar mill built by an American socialist colony in 1893.
Named in 1596 for the Count of Monterrey, then viceroy of New Spain.
It is Mexico’s industrial capital, with the highest income per head of any large Mexican city.
The Cerro de la Silla, a saddle-shaped mountain, stands over it and is the city’s emblem.
"Large tower" — named for a watchtower built against raids.
It forms one urban area with Gómez Palacio and Lerdo, called La Laguna.
A massacre of about 300 Chinese residents here in 1911 was one of the worst episodes of the revolution.
Named for Francisco Gómez Palacio, a nineteenth-century Durango politician.
It sits across the Nazas river from Torreón, in a different state.
The Mapimí Silent Zone north of it is a desert patch with a long-running local legend about radio interference.
From a diminutive of salto, a waterfall or jump — for a stream that fell nearby.
It is the oldest town in north-east Mexico, founded in 1577.
Its sarapes, woven blankets in bright bands, are the classic Mexican design, and it now builds cars for several makers.
From Nahuatl colhuacan, "place of those who have ancestors" or "of the crooked hill".
It is the capital of Sinaloa and the centre of Mexico’s vegetable exports.
Its botanical garden holds a permanent collection of contemporary sculpture among the plants.
Named by a Basque founder in 1563 after Durango in the Basque Country, whose own name means "beyond the water".
Its dry canyons stood in for the American West in dozens of films, and John Wayne shot many of his here.
The Sierra Madre Occidental crossing it holds the Espinazo del Diablo, a road along a knife-edge ridge.
Named for Guadalupe Victoria, the first president of Mexico.
It sits at the foot of the Sierra Madre Oriental, with the El Cielo biosphere reserve nearby.
That reserve is where tropical, desert and temperate forests meet, which makes for unusual bird lists.
From Huastec tam-piko, "place of otters" or "place of dogs".
Mexico’s oil boom began here in 1901, and the city was briefly one of the world’s great oil ports.
B. Traven set The Treasure of the Sierra Madre in and around it.
St Louis plus Potosí — the Bolivian silver mountain, borrowed as a boast that this one would be as rich.
Real de Catorce here is a semi-abandoned silver town reached through a 2.3 km tunnel.
Huasteca Potosina, its eastern half, is waterfalls and turquoise rivers, and the Wixárika make a 400 km pilgrimage across the state each year.
"Hot waters", for the thermal springs the city was founded on in 1575.
The smallest mainland state, and much of its old city is undermined by tunnels nobody has fully mapped.
Its San Marcos fair is the oldest and largest in Mexico, running since 1828.
From Nahuatl tepictli, "hard stone" or "solid place".
It is the capital of Nayarit and sits below the Sangangüey volcano.
The Wixárika (Huichol) sell yarn paintings and beadwork here, made with peyote visions.
From Maya kaan kun, "nest of snakes" or "place of the golden snake".
It was an uninhabited sandbar with three caretakers in 1970, when a computer model picked it as the best site for a resort.
It now receives more international visitors than any other city in Latin America.
Named for León in Spain — León de los Aldama in full.
It makes most of Mexico’s shoes and leather goods.
Its hot-air balloon festival is the largest in Latin America.
Named for Mérida in Spain, because its Maya ruins reminded the conquistadors of that city’s Roman ones.
It was built with the stones of T'hó, the Maya city that stood on the site.
Henequen fibre made it so rich around 1900 that it was said to have more millionaires than anywhere in Mexico.
From a Purépecha or Nahuatl word, possibly "place of low houses".
It is Mexico’s strawberry capital and celebrates it with a festival.
It sits in the Bajío, the fertile basin that was colonial Mexico’s granary.
From Arabic wadi al-hijarah, "river of stones" — named for Guadalajara in Spain, which the Moors named.
Mariachi, tequila, the charreada rodeo and the wide sombrero all come from this region.
It is Mexico’s second city and holds the largest book fair in the Spanish-speaking world.
Probably Purépecha k'erhi-iretarhu, "place of the great town", though a Nahuatl derivation about a ball game is also offered.
Its aqueduct of 74 arches, built in the 1720s, still frames the city, and the historic centre is a UNESCO site.
Mexico's 1917 constitution was written here, and Maximilian was executed on a hill just outside in 1867.
Possibly from Basque zelaia, "flat land" — many of its founders were Basque.
It is famous throughout Mexico for cajeta, a caramel made from goat’s milk.
Obregón lost his arm at the battle of Celaya in 1915, one of the decisive fights of the revolution.
"Rich pool" — named for a pool where oil seeped to the surface.
The field found here in 1930 was one of Mexico’s largest and drove the 1938 nationalisation of oil.
El Tajín nearby is a UNESCO site with a pyramid of 365 niches, one for each day of the year.
From Nahuatl patlachuican, "narrow place" or "place of silver".
Cornish miners came here in 1824, and their pasties became pastes, now the town’s speciality.
They also brought football: Pachuca is Mexico’s oldest club, founded in 1901.
From Nahuatl tzompanco, "place of the skull rack" — the tzompantli where skulls were displayed.
Its lake is one of the last remnants of the lake system that once filled the Valley of Mexico.
Mexico City’s new Felipe Ángeles airport was built at Santa Lucía nearby.
Renamed in 1828 for José María Morelos, who was born in it; it was Valladolid before.
Its pink stone colonial centre is a UNESCO site, and its aqueduct has 253 arches.
Its conservatory, founded in 1743, is the oldest music school in the Americas.
From Nahuatl xalli apan, "on the sandy water" — a spring in sandy ground.
Its anthropology museum holds the best collection of Olmec art, including several colossal heads.
It is called the city of flowers, and grows much of Mexico’s coffee in the hills around it.
From Mexica, the Aztecs’ own name for themselves — the city and the country share it.
It is built on the drained lake bed of Tenochtitlán and sinks up to 50 cm a year in places.
Its Zócalo is one of the largest city squares in the world, laid over the Aztec ceremonial precinct.
From Purépecha urani, "where everything flows" or "place of flowering trees".
It is the avocado capital of the world; Michoacán grows most of the global supply.
The Paricutín volcano nearby rose out of a cornfield in 1943 and grew 424 m in a year while farmers watched.
Named for Nezahualcóyotl, "fasting coyote", the poet-king of Texcoco who died in 1472.
It was built on the dry bed of Lake Texcoco from the 1940s by people with nowhere else to go.
It went from salt flats to over a million people in about thirty years.
From Nahuatl texcalli, "place of maize tortillas" or of crags, depending on which reading you take.
The smallest state, and the one that allied with Cortés against the Aztecs — which is why its people were never conquered and got privileges the rest did not.
Cacaxtla in it holds battle murals in Maya style, painted around 650, among the best-preserved in Mesoamerica.
From Nahuatl tollocan, "place of the god Tolo" or "place of rushes".
The highest large city in Mexico at 2,660 m, with the Nevado de Toluca volcano above it.
That volcano has two lakes inside its crater, of the Sun and the Moon.
"True cross" — Cortés landed on Good Friday 1519 and named the first Spanish town in the mainland Americas for it.
Everything Spain took out of Mexico left through this port for three hundred years, and everything African and Caribbean came in: son jarocho music is the result.
Pico de Orizaba on its border is Mexico's highest mountain at 5,636 m, and vanilla was first cultivated by the Totonac here.
Short for Puebla de los Ángeles, "town of the angels" — founded in 1531 as a Spanish town with no indigenous settlement underneath it.
Cinco de Mayo commemorates the 1862 battle here, where a smaller Mexican force beat the French army.
Cholula beside it has the largest pyramid by volume in the world, with a church built on top of it — the Spanish thought it was a hill.
A Spanish mangling of Nahuatl cuauhnahuac, "near the trees" — they heard "cow horn".
Its mild weather made it the retreat of Aztec emperors, then Cortés, then Maximilian.
It is called the city of eternal spring, and Malcolm Lowry set Under the Volcano here.
From Nahuatl ahuilizapan, "place of pleasant waters".
Pico de Orizaba above it is Mexico’s highest mountain at 5,636 m and the third highest in North America.
Its 1907 textile strike at Río Blanco was crushed by the army and is counted a precursor of the revolution.
From Nahuatl coatzacualco, "where the snake hides" — said to be where Quetzalcoatl departed.
It is the main port of Mexico’s petrochemical industry.
It sits on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, the narrowest part of Mexico, about 200 km across.
"Beautiful town" — Villahermosa de San Juan Bautista in full.
Its La Venta park displays Olmec colossal heads moved there from a site threatened by oil drilling.
It is one of the wettest and most humid cities in Mexico.
From Nahuatl huaxyacac, "at the nose of the guaje tree", a pod-bearing tree still common there.
The most linguistically diverse state in Mexico: sixteen indigenous language groups, and many of its towns govern by customary law rather than party politics.
Monte Albán above the city was the Zapotec capital, and the state is the home of mole, mezcal and Día de Muertos as the world pictures it.
From Nahuatl acatl poloa, "where the reeds were destroyed".
It was the Pacific end of the Manila galleon route for 250 years, bringing Asian silk and porcelain across two oceans.
Its La Quebrada divers have leapt 35 m into a narrow inlet since 1934, timing the jump to the swell.
Tuxtla is from Nahuatl tochtlan, "place of rabbits"; Gutiérrez was a state governor.
The Sumidero canyon beside it has walls up to 1,000 m high and is on the state coat of arms.
It is the capital of Chiapas and the gateway to the Maya sites at Palenque.
